title: Strong northern lights forecast. Clouds will make viewing difficult
excerpt: The northern lights could be visible overhead Friday and Saturday, if you can get away from cloud cover.
content:
Nov. 6, 2026, 10:45 a.m. ET

Northern Michigan and the Upper Peninsula could see strong northern lights Friday night, Nov. 6, but they'll likely be blocked by poor weather this weekend.

On Friday night, Nov. 6, NOAA predicts a G1 geomagnetic storm will produce a Kp index of 5, and on Saturday night, Nov. 7, a G0 geomagnetic storm is expected to produce a Kp index of 4, leading to northern lights shining in northern Michigan and U.P. skies.

However, local National Weather Service offices predict clouds overnight Nov. 6 and Nov. 7, and in some areas on Friday night, Nov. 6, rain and snow, across the region, which could disrupt northern lights viewing chances.

Kp is an index used to indicate the severity of the global magnetic disturbances in near-Earth space, NOAA said. Kp ratings increase from zero to 9. NOAA is predicting minor geomagnetic storm impacts.

Consider heading to one of Michigan's dark sky areas in regions with clear, dry conditions, for a closer look at the lunar eclipse and colorful auroras.

Here's what to know about the northern lights outlook.

When could the northern lights be visible?

The northern lights could be visible in northern Michigan and the U.P. Friday night, Nov. 6 and Saturday night, Nov. 7, per the SWPC. NOAA is predicting a G1 geomagnetic storm Nov. 6 producing a Kp index of 5 and on Nov. 7 a G0 geomagnetic storm producing a Kp index of 4.

However, clouds, and in some areas, rain or snow, could limit visibility, according to forecasts from local NWS offices in Michigan.

What are the northern lights?

The northern lights, or aurora borealis, are waves of light created when the solar wind strikes the atmosphere, creating a display of moving lights in the night sky.

Why do the northern lights have different colors?

The color of the aurora depends on which gas is being excited by the electrons and on how much energy is being exchanged, NASA said.

Oxygen emits either a greenish-yellow light (the most familiar color of the aurora) or a red light; nitrogen generally gives off a blue light. The oxygen and nitrogen molecules also emit ultraviolet light, which can only be detected by special cameras on satellites.

Can't see the northern lights? Use your phone

If you're having trouble seeing the northern lights with the naked eye, try using your phone camera in night mode and hold still while capturing the photo. You might be surprised at what's dancing in the sky.
